name: Sofar Ocean Technologies (formerly OpenROV)
subcategory: ocean sensing: open-source ROV kits (OpenROV), then Spotter buoy network, marine weather and voyage-optimization software
origin_detail: David Lang and Eric Stackpole, then a NASA engineering intern, founded OpenROV in 2011 as a garage-built, low-cost open-source underwater robot. It was shown at World Maker Faire in 2011 and was based mostly in Berkeley, CA. In March 2019 it merged with Spoondrift, maker of the Spotter wave buoy, to form Sofar Ocean Technologies. SolarCity co-founder Peter Rive orchestrated the merger.
openness_notes: Hardware column. OpenROV started as an open-source hardware project. It published CAD for every DIY-kit version (v2.3-v2.8), electronics schematics, laser-cut DXFs and software, and had builders in over 30 countries. The CAD licence is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, which is non-commercial and so does not meet the OSHW definition; that makes the initial 3 borderline 2/3. The later Trident ROV has only an interfacing development kit published (MIT); no full design files were found. Sofar's core products (Spotter, Sentrix, Wayfinder, Marine Weather) carry no open-source statements on its website. Sofar has since opened a peripheral layer: Bristlemouth, 'an open standard delivering plug-and-play hardware interfaces for marine applications', with Apache-2.0 firmware. The current level is 1, with only peripheral parts open.

risk_events: 2019: the merger pivoted the company from open, consumer ROVs to a proprietary ocean-data business. Part of the Series A was earmarked for developing safeguards for Trident drones (TechCrunch).
Customer concentration in government and defence: ONR, US Navy and NOAA appear among its customers and partners (website, 2026).
Open OpenROV design repos have gone unmaintained since 2019-2022 (hardware last updated 2020-02-27; electronics 2022-08-11).
robustness: Sofar is a private, VC-backed company that says it runs 'the largest privately-owned ocean sensor network in the world': 2.5K+ Spotters, 1.5M real-time observations a day and 25M+ hours of observations. Its value sits in proprietary sensors, data and routing software sold to shipping fleets and government. The old OpenROV designs remain public (CC BY-NC-SA) but unmaintained. Bristlemouth spreads interoperability across a multi-partner open standard, though the pages fetched name no governance body.
physical_science_relevance: Directly relevant to oceanography. Spotter buoys supply wave, weather and subsurface observations used by NOAA and the US Navy, and National Geographic was one of the biggest Trident buyers. Bristlemouth aims at plug-and-play interoperability for marine scientific instruments.
openness_effect_assessment: Openness gave OpenROV a global builder community (30+ countries) and early backing ($1.3M from True Ventures and National Geographic). Scale came only after it moved to a ready-to-use ROV and then, through the 2019 merger, to a proprietary sensor-network and data business. Sofar then used openness strategically at the interface layer (Bristlemouth, Apache-2.0 firmware, with ONR, NOAA and philanthropic partners) to grow an ecosystem around its closed core.
key_takeaway: Sofar/OpenROV traces the full arc from open-hardware DIY project to closed, VC-backed data company. It began in 2011 with public CAD under a non-commercial CC licence and a community in 30+ countries. The 2019 merger made it a business of Spotter buoys and data software sold to shipping and the Navy. It closed the product and later opened a standard (Bristlemouth) where interoperability serves it, the 'open the interfaces, close the product' pattern. Its CC BY-NC-SA licence also shows a common open-science compromise that does not meet the OSHW definition. Funding after the 2019 $7M Series A, and any valuation, could not be found without search.
